phoenix-san-francisco-first-place.title: San Francisco scored 18 and still couldn’t shake Phoenix
sections: On July 26 the San Francisco Warriors could have lost a series and still had room to spare. They were six games ahead of Phoenix. On August 19 they scored 18 runs and couldn’t shake the Firebirds. Both clubs finished the night 64–57. Now Phoenix comes to San Francisco for four games, and the winner of Thursday’s opener will have first place to itself.

San Francisco’s lead disappeared during an eight-game losing streak. The first came August 9, when Minneapolis beat San Francisco 6–5. By August 16, three straight losses to Dallas and three more to Atlanta had left the Warriors even with Phoenix. The next night San Francisco took a 1–0 lead into the seventh against Tampa Bay and lost 2–1. Phoenix beat Dallas 3–2 that night and went in front.

The Warriors took their share of first place back on Tuesday with a 6–1 win while Phoenix lost. On Wednesday they put six runs across in the first inning against Tampa Bay. Luke Margalit homered and drove in five in the 18–2 win. San Francisco scored 24 runs in its two wins over the Storm. It had scored 15 in the eight straight losses. The bats have given the Warriors a chance to defend first place at home. The standings gave them no head start.
The game that kept it even

In Phoenix, Stephen Grimes carried a shutout into the ninth against Dallas. By the time he came out with one down, he had allowed three hits and struck out seven. Omar Espinoza got the last two outs. The Firebirds did all their scoring in the fourth, when Alex Monge, acquired from Houston on July 28, homered. Three runs were plenty.

Phoenix has won nine of the clubs’ 15 meetings, but the four played in San Francisco ended two apiece. Los Angeles is two games behind both leaders. When the Firebirds and Warriors meet August 20, one team can finally put a win on its own side of the standings and a loss on the other’s. See who leaves the opener 65–57. For at least one night, the West will belong to that club alone.

claim_map.claim: San Francisco scored 15 runs in eight straight losses from August 9 through August 17.
Phoenix took first on August 17. The Warriors drew even the following night.
San Francisco scored 24 runs in its last two games against Tampa Bay. Margalit drove in five in the 18–2 win.
Stephen Grimes and Omar Espinoza shut out Dallas 3–0. Alex Monge homered in the fourth inning.
Phoenix and San Francisco went into the series tied at 64–57 with Los Angeles two games back.
Phoenix is scheduled at San Francisco for four games starting August 20.

review.question: How did a six-game San Francisco advantage become a tie that Thursday’s opener will break?
review.promise: The lead follows the lost cushion, the Warriors’ brief fall behind Phoenix, and the separate wins that sent both clubs into their meeting at 64–57.
review.sequence: July 26 standings, the August losing streak, the August 17–18 changes of leader, the contrasting August 19 wins, then the first scheduled head-to-head game.
review.stakes: The opener’s winner moves to 65–57 and sole possession of the NBC West. Los Angeles cannot draw even on Thursday.
review.ending: Return for Phoenix at San Francisco, scheduled game 1458 on August 20. The outcome answers who takes first place.

miami-needs-a-game-before-charlotte.title: Miami needs a game before Charlotte comes to town
sections: Miami could sweep Charlotte at home next week and still finish the series in second place. Even after three straight losses in Minneapolis, the Colonels are 69–52 and lead the Hurricanes by four and a half games. Their next meeting is August 27 in Miami. Until then, somebody else has to beat Charlotte for the Hurricanes to close the gap.

Miami knows the price of letting a game get away against Charlotte. The last time they met, on July 26, the Hurricanes took a 4–1 lead into the bottom of the ninth. A single and a triple brought one run home. A sacrifice fly brought in another. With two outs and Miami still ahead 4–3, Nigel Hudson fouled off two pitches, then hit a two-run homer to win it for the Colonels. Charlotte finished the day eight games ahead.

Miami has taken three and a half games off that lead since then. It got one of them this week. While the Colonels were getting swept, Miami won the middle game of its series in San Diego, 4–0. Wednesday offered another opening. Charlotte lost 9–3, but the Hurricanes went into the ninth trailing 6–2. They scored twice and left San Diego with a 64–56 record.
Six games to change the margin

Both contenders have six games scheduled before they see each other. Miami plays four at Atlanta, then gets Tampa Bay twice at home. Charlotte plays four at Tampa Bay and two at Atlanta. The same two opponents stand between the contenders and their August 27 meeting. They have given them very different trouble.

The Kings have beaten Miami nine times in 15 meetings. In the last one, Miami led 4–1 going into the ninth. Atlanta tied it with three runs, and Gerardo Rodriguez homered to open the 11th for a 5–4 win. Charlotte, meanwhile, has gone 11–4 against Tampa Bay. The Hurricanes open Thursday against the club that took that July game away from them. To gain ground that night, they need help from the club Charlotte has beaten most often in the East.

Watch the two finals together on August 20. A Miami win in Atlanta and a Charlotte loss at Tampa Bay cut the lead to three and a half, small enough for Miami to pass Charlotte in a four-game series. Reverse those results and the lead grows to five and a half. The series in Miami is a week away. What it can settle is already being played for.

claim_map.claim: On July 26 Nigel Hudson's two-out, two-run homer finished Charlotte's four-run ninth and 5–4 win over Miami.
Charlotte lost all three in Minneapolis while Miami won once at San Diego, gaining a game to finish four and a half behind.
Atlanta tied its most recent game against Miami with three in the ninth and won on Gerardo Rodriguez’s leadoff homer in the 11th.
Each contender has six games against Atlanta and Tampa Bay before meeting the other. The August 20 finals can move Charlotte’s lead from four and a half to three and a half or five and a half.
Charlotte’s next visit to Miami is a four-game series opening August 27. At the present gap even a Miami sweep would leave Charlotte half a game ahead.

review.question: What does Miami have to change before its home series can put it in front of Charlotte?
review.promise: The lead gives the reason a full game matters. The previous head-to-head ending gives that arithmetic a face in Nigel Hudson.
review.sequence: The August 19 standings establish the problem; July 26 explains the starting margin; the two recent road series show what Miami has recovered; the remaining schedule puts Atlanta and Tampa Bay in the race.
review.stakes: With a 4½-game lead, Charlotte could absorb a four-game sweep and stay ahead. A one-game gain in the meantime puts a lead within reach of that series.
review.ending: Read Miami at Atlanta and Charlotte at Tampa Bay together on August 20. Opposite results make the lead 3½ or 5½ games.
